title: The traveler's prayer
hookLine: a short prayer for safety, said setting out on a journey

lines: A CARD IN A PASSENGER'S HAND.
cards: Watch a plane taxi toward the runway, and sometimes you'll see it: a passenger with a small laminated card, lips moving. Or a driver pulling onto the highway, glancing at a card tucked behind the sun visor.
Some Jewish car keychains even have a tiny version printed on them. It's the same few lines, said once at the start of a journey.
A prayer that's older than cars, planes or highways, from a time when the dangers on the road had teeth and swords.

teach.b: It's called Tefillat HaDerech, the prayer of the road. The Talmud, in Berakhot 29b, says that anyone setting out on a journey should say it, and it gives the wording, close to what's said now.

In paraphrase: may it be Your will to lead us toward peace, to guide our steps toward peace, to bring us to where we're going in life, joy and peace, and to save us from every enemy and ambush on the way.

The dangers named were real for travelers then: bandits, wild animals, the long stretch between towns. The Talmud records a small detail that's still followed. Abaye said to say it in the plural, lead us, not lead me.

teach.h: US, NOT ME, ON THE HIGHWAY.
teach.b: Even alone in a car, you pray as part of a group. There are rules about when. Many say it once you've left the city behind you, not in your driveway, and only once for each day of travel, even if the trip has many legs.
And the Talmud tells of Elijah advising a sage named Rav Yehudah: before you set out on the road, consult your Creator. The prayer is short on purpose.
It's meant to be said by someone with a bag on their shoulder and somewhere to be.
Many add verses after it, and some add lines from Psalm 121, a psalm about the road: "The LORD shall guard thy going out and thy coming in, from this time forth and for ever."
Going out and coming in. Every trip has both.

how: Many Jews say Tefillat HaDerech once per day of travel, after leaving their town, on road trips, flights and long journeys; printed cards and keychains with the text are common.

games.q: you're driving alone across the country. the trip has five stops today. how many times do you say the traveler's prayer, and how?
o: five times, once per stop, in the singular.
once for the day, in the plural.
only if the road looks dangerous.
games.why: many say it once per day of travel, and Abaye taught the plural: even alone, you pray as one of many.

practice: Picture yourself at the door before your next trip, even a short one, and find the sentence you'll say as you step out.
If you pray, it could be the Talmud's own wish, toward peace, or the psalm's going out and coming in; if not, a simple hope that you, and everyone on the road, get where you're going.

wordCard.voice: Tefillat HaDerech. The prayer of the road. Said once a day when setting out, in the plural, asking to arrive in life, joy and peace.
